abstract: Approximation semantics capture the observable behaviour of λ-terms. Böhm Trees and Taylor Expansion are its two central paradigms, related by the Commutation Theorem. While these notions are well understood in Call-by-Name (CbN), they have only recently been developed for Call-by-Value (CbV), which motivate the search for a unified approximation framework. The Bang-calculus provides such a framework: it subsumes both CbN and CbV through linear-logic translations and enjoys robust rewriting properties. Via translations, our results recover the CbN and CbV cases within a single unifying framework capturing infinitary and resource-sensitive semantics.

    1    Introduction

A central approach to λ-calculus semantics is program approximation theory, which captures
program behaviour, finitarily or infinitarily, offering a characterization of “meaningful” terms.
    In Call-by-Name (CbN), meaningful terms are the solvable ones, i.e. those reducing
to identity under some“testing context”. In Call-by-Value (CbV), meaningfulness is given
by scrutability 1 , which only requires reduction to a value and is strictly finer. Among
approximation techniques, evaluation trees and Taylor Expansions are the most influential.
Böhm trees introduced by Barendregt [10] are the seminal evaluation trees. They associate
to each λ-term a (possibly infinite) tree whose nodes describe successive approximations of
the term’s head normal form, or ⊥ – canonical term meaning nonsense, or divergence – when
none exists, thus capturing its asymptotic CbN behaviour. Böhm trees were related to the
notion of solvability of CbN terms by the fact that a term is solvable if and only if its Böhm
tree is not ⊥.

           Ehrhard and Regnier later introduced Taylor expansion [23], inspired by the differential λ-
       calculus [22] and relational semantics [30]. Taylor expansion unfolds a λ-term into an (infinite)
       formal sum of resource terms underlying the linear-use of resources during computations,
       rather than progressively revealing their shape as Böhm trees do.
           The Commutation Theorem [23, Corollary 35] states that normalizing the Taylor expansion
       of a term yields exactly the Taylor expansion of its Böhm tree. Taylor expansions can
       then be understood as a resource-sensitive version of Böhm trees. Originally proved for
       the CbN λ-calculus, this result provides a deep bridge between infinitary semantics and
       differential/resource semantics.
           While Taylor expansions for the CbV calculus were already studied in [15, 19], the
       development of CbV Böhm trees remained open until Kerinec’s PhD work [28, 27]. Those
       Böhm trees have the same commutation theorem with Taylor expansion as in the CbN case.
       They also respect the same relation with scrutability as CbN Böhm trees do with solvability.
       This emphasizes that scrutability is the appropriate notion of meaningfulness in CbV. However,
       this result is obtained in an alternative version of the original Plotkin CbV, which is known
       to have issues due to the βv -reduction being “too weak”. Concretely, unlike in CbN, CbV
       reduction may get stuck: redexes can be blocked since their argument is in normal form but
       not a value. This phenomenon prevents a straightforward infinitary unfolding analogous to
       the CbN case.
           The aforementioned CbV Böhm trees are defined in the λσv -calculus from [15], where the
       βv -reduction is extended with permutation rules, the so-called σ-rules, originating from the
       translation of λ-terms to proof-nets [26]. Another way to solve the CbV issue, also coming
       from proof-nets, is using a distance-based CbV calculus: distant CbV (dCbV)2 [2, 1, 3]. In this
       system, substitutions may be frozen thanks to explicit substitutions, written M [N/x], which
       do not correspond to (effective) substitutions, but instead represent substitutions that are
       yet to be evaluated. The rewriting rules then act at a distance with respect to the explicit
       substitutions.
           The divergence between CbN and CbV has historically required separate developments
       of most semantic notions. Such a duplication naturally called for a unifying perspective.
       Call-by-Push-Value (CbPV) [31] provides precisely this, reconciling typed CbN and CbV within
       a single calculus structured around a clear distinction between values and computations.
       CbPV later gave rise to its untyped analogue Bang-calculus (Bang) [21], by use of Linear
       Logic [20]. Both CbN and CbV arise within the Bang-calculus via Girard’s translations of the
       intuitionistic arrow into Linear Logic [25], making it a natural setting in which to seek a
       uniform approximation theory. The Bang-calculus is then an extension of the λ-calculus with
       two new constructs: !M (pronounced “bang M ”) which freezes the computation of M , and
       der(M ) which unfreezes it. Both CbN and CbV can then be translated into the Bang-calculus,
       which simulates their rewriting strategies within a single rewriting system.
           However, the Bang-calculus exhibits the same issue as CbV: ill-formed redexes may block
       evaluation. One might expect that adapting the σ-rules to the Bang-calculus would solve
       this issue; however, while the CbV calculus with σ-rules is confluent, this is not the case
       for the Bang calculus [21, Sec.2.3]. Confluence can be recovered modulo an equivalence
       relation contained in the σ-equivalence generated by the σ-rules, but this requires working
       modulo said equivalence. Another solution to this problem is to consider the distance variant
       (dBang) [14], similar to the distant variant of CbV. This allows us to work without the σ-rules

It has also been used in unifying multiple results for dCbN and dCbV. For instance, in [8]

to the dCbN and dCbV setting using the translations into dBang3 . Similarly, the notion of

dBang-calculus remains largely underdeveloped.
    A recent work by Mazza & Dufour tried to close that gap [18]: they developed a generic
notion of Böhm tree and Taylor expansion for a language called Proc, representing untyped
proof structures. They showed how any language that can be embedded into Proc in a
“nice way” inherits the notions of Böhm tree and Taylor expansion from Proc, and their
commutation Theorem. In particular, dBang admit such an embedding. However, no notion
of meaningfulness exists in Proc and it is not clear how to relate the results from CbN and
CbV with the notion developed in [18].

1.1       Contributions
We develop a theory of approximation of the distance Bang-calculus (dBang). To this
end we recall the definitions and main results of dBang from [29, 8, 14] in Section 2. We
start by developing the Taylor expansion of dBang (Section 2.2) where we introduce the
resource calculus (Section 2.2.1) and define the approximation relation (Section 2.2.2) and
establish a simulation result between dBang and its approximants in the Taylor expansion
(Theorem 21). We next develop the Böhm approximants of dBang (Section 2.3)4 and prove a
commutation theorem between the Taylor Expansion of Böhm trees and the Taylor normal
form (Theorem 46).
    We establish the soundness of our definitions with regard to the standard notion of Böhm
trees and Taylor Expansions in the distance call-by-name (dCbN) and distance call-by-value
(dCbV) λ-calculus by translating these systems into dBang (Section 3), in particular, we show
that the Böhm trees of a term M in dCbN (respectively dCbV) are the same as its translation
into dBang (Theorem 59). We show a similar result for Taylor expansion (Lemmas 54 and
Corollaries 55).
    Finally, we establish the commutation result for both dCbN and dCbV as a consequence of
the dBang commutation theorem 60.

There is no necessity to define specific resource calculi, as δBang fits well as a target of
usual Taylor expansion (CbN [24] and cbv [19]), with a straightforward adaptation to distant
setting.

2.3    Approximation trees
A classical way to approximate λ-terms is through evaluation trees, which can be seen as
infinitary normal forms. The evaluation tree of a λ-term corresponds to the limit of a sequence
of increasingly precise approximants of this λ-term. Those approximants are terms in normal
forms, but using potentially a specific subterm ⊥, representing an undefined computation.
When reducing the λ-term some subterms become stable under further reductions, these
subterms are precisely those captured by approximants.
    Different comparable evaluation trees coexist. The original and best-known ones are
Böhm trees. They have been introduced in the CbN paradigm where they intersect with
numerous notions. Indeed, they give a precise classification of λ-terms in regard of their
operationnal behaviour.
    In CbN, using all partial normal forms (possibly containing ⊥) as approximants, corres-
ponds to Lévy-Longo trees [32]. Böhm trees use a restriction on this set of approximants,
so that unsolvable terms have an empty Böhm tree. This restriction is based on restricting
approximants to (partial) head normal forms, since being solvable is equivalent to having a
head normal form. Lévy-Longo trees instead rely on weak head normal forms. In fact, it only
leads to the suppression of “stupid” approximants such as λx⊥. Böhm trees and Lévy-Longo
trees differ essentially in their treatment of abstractions over undefined computations and
therefore share similar properties. Among others, they both satisfy variants of the Commut-
ation Theorem, which states that Taylor expansion of the Böhm tree of a term is equal to its
Taylor normal form [24].

         5     Conclusion and Discussions
        We developed an approximation theory for the distant dBang-calculus, defining approximation
        trees and Taylor expansion and relating them to meaningfulness and to each other. These
        results are part of a wider effort to generalize the theory of the CbN and CbV λ-calculi. And
        indeed, we retrieve similar results in distant CbN and distant CbV, via translations in dBang.
            Future work includes extending meaningfulness to proof structures, pursuing Dufour
        and Mazza’s work [18] using non-inductive variants of classical approximation notions (in
        particular, their Böhm trees do not have an actual tree structure since approximations cannot
        be described through an tree-like inductive syntax). Also, we mentioned in Section 4 an
        open question about the possibility to characterize a significant fragment of dBang for which
        meaningful terms coincide with terms having a non-empty Taylor normal form; this line of
        work should be explored to develop the general understanding of dBang.
